utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-R77.4, the Prosecutor versus Astrit Haraqija and Bajrush Morina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I see that Mr. Haraqija is present, as is his counsel, Mr. Khan. Same for Mr. Morina and Mr. Dieckmann; and Mr. Saxon is present on behalf of the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber is sitting today to deliver its Judgement in the case of The Prosecutor versus Astrit Haraqija and Bajrush Morina. For the purposes of this hearing, the Trial Chamber will briefly summarize the procedural history of the case, the applicable law, certain submissions of the parties, and the Chamber's findings. We would like to emphasise that this is but a summary and that the only authoritative account of the Trial Chamber's findings is the written Judgement which will be made available at the end of the session. I start with the procedural history and the indictment. The indictment against Astrit Haraqija and Bajrush Morina was filed by the Office of the Prosecutor on the 8th of January, 2008, and was confirmed on the 12th of February, 2008. It alleges that, in July and August 2007, the accused, acting on their own initiative or at the request of others, incited or committed contempt of the Tribunal by having knowingly and wilfully interfered with the administration of justice by interfering with a protected witness in the case of the Prosecutor versus Haradinaj et al. The protected witness will be called Witness 2 for the purposes of this Judgement. The indictment alleges that the accused knew that Witness 2 was an important witness in the Haradinaj et al. case. It further alleges that in early July 2007, Astrit Haraqija, then Minister for Culture, Youth and Sport, instructed Bajrush Morina, who knew Witness 2, to organise a meeting in order to persuade Witness 2 not to testify against Ramush Haradinaj. The indictment alleges that although Astrit Haraqija initially planned to travel with Bajrush Morina to meet Witness 2, eventually only Bajrush Morina met him. According to the indictment, on the 10th and the 11th of July, 2007, Bajrush Morina and Witness 2 had two meetings, which were recorded by the police, in which Bajrush Morina pressured Witness 2 not to testify against Ramush Haradinaj. As an official of the Ministry for Culture, Youth and Sport at that time, Bajrush Morina required permission for his trip abroad. According to the indictment, the expenses were paid by the ministry. Based on the foregoing, the Prosecution has charged Astrit Haraqija with one count of contempt of the Tribunal, punishable under 77(A)(iv) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal, or, in the alternative with one count of incitement to contempt of the Tribunal, punishable under 77(A)(iv) and (B) of the Rules, and Bajrush Morina with one count of contempt of the Tribunal punishable under Rule 77(A)(iv) of the Rules. The trial was conducted from the 8th of September, 2008, to the 11th of September, 2008. During the trial, the Trial Chamber admitted 39 exhibits into evidence. It also received evidence from a total of five Prosecution witnesses and four witnesses for the Haraqija Defence. Astrit Haraqija also made a statement pursuant to Rule 84 bis and testified as a witness. Counsel for Bajrush Morina did not call any witnesses. I will now move to the relevant law as applied in this case. Despite the Statute's silence on contempt of the Tribunal, it is firmly established that the Tribunal possesses an inherent jurisdiction to prosecute and punish contempt. This inherent jurisdiction derives from the Tribunal's judicial power to ensure that its exercise of the jurisdiction given to it by the Statute is not frustrated and that its basic judicial functions are safeguarded. Both accused are charged pursuant to Rule 77(A)(iv) of the Rules. This provision provides that: "The Tribunal, in the exercise of its inherent power, may hold in contempt those who knowingly and wilfully intensive with its administration of justice, including any person who: "(iv) threatens, intimidates, causes any injury or offers a bribe to, or otherwise interferes with, a witness who is giving, has given, or is about to give evidence in proceedings before a Chamber, or a potential witness ..." A "threat" is defined as a communicated intent to inflict harm or damage of some kind to a witness and/or the witness's property, or to a third person, and/or his property, so as to influence or overcome the will of the witness to whom the threat is addressed. "Intimidation" consists of acts or culpable omissions likely to constitute direct, indirect, or potential threats to a witness, which may interfere with or influence the witness's testimony. "Otherwise interfering with a witness" encompasses acts or omissions, other than threatening, intimidating, causing injury or offering a bribe, which are capable of and likely to deter a witness from giving full and truthful testimony or in any other way influence the nature of the witness's evidence. The person otherwise interfering with a witness must have acted willingly and with the knowledge that his conduct was likely to deter or influence the witness. In the alternative, Astrit Haraqija is also charged with incitement to commit contempt of the Tribunal pursuant to Rule 77(B) of the Rules, according to which any person who knowingly and wilfully encourages and/or persuades another person to commit any act described in Rule 77(A) of the Rules shall be subject to the same penalties as one who commits the act. The requirement of corroboration, I will now turn to the question raised by the Haraqija Defence whether evidence relating to the acts and conducts of Astrit Haraqija in Bajrush Morina's suspect interview that was admitted into evidence requires corroboration; and if so, whether the corroborating evidence may originate from the same witness. If the answer to both questions is in the affirmative, then the Trial Chamber must also consider the extent to which its findings may permissibly rely upon a statement which has not been subject to cross-examination. The Appeals Chamber has confirmed the principle that a conviction based solely, or in a decisive manner, on the depositions of a witness, whom the accused has had no opportunity to examine or to have examined either during the investigation or at trial, constitutes an unacceptable infringement of the right of an accused to a fair trial. The right to confront witnesses applies to depositions made against an accused, both by regular witnesses as well as co-accused. Therefore evidence of a witness who has not been subject to cross-examination will require sufficient corroboration by significant evidence if relied upon to establish a conviction. As the Rules and the Tribunal's jurisprudence are bereft of any case which deal with the requirements in relation to corroborative evidence, the Trial Chamber analysed the approaches taken by several national jurisdictions in that respect. As the Trial Chamber is not bound by any national rules of corroboration, it did so only in looking for guidance. From the analysis that can be found in the Judgement, the Trial Chamber concluded that while some jurisdictions require that in order to be used as corroboration, the evidence must come from a separate and independent source, others take a less technical approach, requiring only that the corroborating evidence link a defendant with the commission of the crime, but not necessarily originate from a different source. Mindful of its duty to apply rules of evidence which will best favour a fair determination of the matter before it and are consonant with the spirit of the Statute and the general principles of law, the Trial Chamber determined that, in order for a piece of evidence to be able to corroborate non-cross-examined evidence, it must not only induce a strong belief of truthfulness of the latter, i.e., enhance its probative value, but must also be obtained in an independent manner. Rejecting a technical approach to this issue, the Trial Chamber held that corroborating evidence might include pieces of evidence that, although originating from the same source, arose under different circumstances, at different times, and for different purposes. Such evidence would indeed meet the requirement of sufficient corroboration, which is aimed at preventing an encroachment of the rights of the accused. I will now address the Trial Chamber's findings in relation to the responsibility of Bajrush Morina. The Trial Chamber heard evidence establishing that Bajrush Morina contacted Witness 2 on July the 2nd of 2007, and subsequently travelled to meet him on the 10th and the 11th of July. During the meetings, Bajrush Morina told Witness 2 that he had been sent by Astrit Haraqija to ask Witness 2 not to testify against Ramush Haradinaj in order to save Haradinaj. Bajrush Morina also told Witness 2 that other witnesses who had testified in the Haradinaj et al. case before the Tribunal were subsequently killed. The Trial Chamber found that the evidence consistently shows that Bajrush Morina knew that Witness 2 was about to testify in the Haradinaj et al. case. The Trial Chamber dismissed the submission by the Defence that the Prosecution failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Bajrush Morina's conduct was likely to dissuade Witness 2 from giving evidence. Although the conduct of Bajrush Morina took the form of amicable advice and was staged in a friendly atmosphere, it was clear that Bajrush Morina's words were intended and could only be understood as a strong and unequivocal call on Witness 2 to refrain from testifying in the Haradinaj et al. case. In the Trial Chamber's view, such behaviour constituted intimidation, an interference of a nature proscribed by 77(A)(iv) of the Rules. Bajrush Morina's failure to dissuade Witness 2 from testifying was immaterial for establishing Bajrush Morina's responsibility. Likewise, the lack of motive alleged by the Defence could not have an impact in this case. Just as the existence of a motive to commit a crime is in itself of minimal, if any, probative value, that the accused has committed it, the absence of a motive cannot disprove facts established through reliable evidence. The absence of a motive may, however, call for further exploration of the convincing potential of the evidence before establishing that the crime was committed and that the accused committed it. In the present case, however, the evidence was strong and convincing. The Trial Chamber therefore found that Bajrush Morina's conduct constituted contempt of the Tribunal purpose to 77(A)(iv) of the Rules. I will now move to the Trial Chamber's findings in relation to the responsibility of Astrit Haraqija. The Trial Chamber first addressed the Prosecution's submissions, that, on the 2nd of July, 2007, Astrit Haraqija met Bajrush Morina at cultural event in Peja and instructed him to organise a meeting with Witness 2. While the evidence was not conclusive, the Trial Chamber found that the date and place of such a conversation is immaterial for Astrit Haraqija's responsibility and subsequently turned to the question whether it had been established that Astrit Haraqija directed Bajrush Morina to interfere with Witness 2. The Trial Chamber recalled its findings that Bajrush Morina's conduct constituted contempt of the Tribunal. Whereas Astrit Haraqija's involvement follows most directly from Bajrush Morina's suspect interview and the intercepts of the meetings between Bajrush Morina and Witness 2, the Trial Chamber found that it was also established by the totality of the evidence. The Trial Chamber was mindful that most pieces of evidence ultimately originated from Bajrush Morina. However, it considered them to be independent from the suspect interview, as well as from each other, since they arose under different circumstances, at different times, and were generated for different purposes, as is explained in more detail in the Judgement. In addition to regarding the different categories of evidence as sufficiently independent from each other and thus being capable of corroborating the suspect interview, the Trial Chamber also found that there was a higher -- a high degree of consistency throughout the entire evidence regarding Astrit Haraqija's involvement. Moreover, the Trial Chamber found that the evidence negated the alternative scenario in which Bajrush Morina would have consistently implicated Astrit Haraqija under all circumstances and at all times when the incriminating evidence was generated. Moreover, Astrit Haraqija's diary and other travel commitments did it not contradict the evidence concerning Astrit Haraqija's involvement, since they do not contain any commitments on the relevant dates, which would be capable of raising a reasonable doubt as to Astrit Haraqija's participation. Finally, considerations of an alternative motive for Bajrush Morina to meet with Witness 2 in order to interfere with his testimony also did not raise a reasonable doubt as to Astrit Haraqija's responsibility. The Trial Chamber found it highly unlikely that Bajrush Morina would have undertaken the trip on his own, considering his personal and financial background. Astrit Haraqija, on the other hand, had become involved in the Defence of Ramush Haradinaj in the context of his political position within the Democratic Alliance of Kosovo, the LDK and the coalition government under Haradinaj. Furthermore, Astrit Haraqija had repeatedly expressed discontent and lack of understanding with respect to the trial of Kosovars, such as Ramush Haradinaj, before this Tribunal. In conclusion, the Trial Chamber was satisfied that the only reasonable inference to be drawn from the evidence in its totality, considering its mutually corroborating linkages and the circumstances as a whole, is that Astrit Haraqija knew that Witness 2 was a witness in the Haradinaj et al. trial before the Tribunal, and instructed Bajrush Morina to call on Witness 2 with the specific task of interfering with his testimony. Although Astrit Haraqija did not personally meet or interact with Witness 2, the Trial Chamber found that the evidence established beyond a reasonable doubt that Astrit Haraqija, knowing that Witness 2 was about to give evidence before the Tribunal, exercised his influence over Bajrush Morina, who accepted Haraqija's authority and followed his directions. Therefore, the Trial Chamber found that Haraqija's conduct formed an integral part of Bajrush Morina's criminal conduct and thus constitutes contempt of the Tribunal, pursuant to 77(A)(iv) of the Rules. I will now turn to the Trial Chamber's considerations of the sentences to be imposed. The Trial Chamber noted in respect of both accused that the intimidation of witnesses is particularly grave among the possible ways of interfering with the administration of justice. This assessment of gravity also took into account the importance of ensuring that the atmosphere of trials before the Tribunal allow for the proper administration of justice by protecting witnesses from interference. Therefore, the Trial Chamber did not further consider the particular situation, which the Trial Chamber in the Haradinaj et al. case faced, in securing witness testimony in an atmosphere that many witnesses perceived to be unsafe as an aggravating circumstance. As an aggravating circumstance, the Trial Chamber found that Astrit Haraqija abused his high position in the structure of the government to put pressure on an employee of his ministry. As mitigating circumstances for Bajrush Morina, the Trial Chamber considered his good character, the absence of a prior criminal record, and his family situation. The Trial Chamber also considered the fact that, in committing the contempt of the Tribunal, Bajrush Morina was pressured by Astrit Haraqija and that Bajrush Morina was reluctant to carry out what Astrit Haraqija had told him to do, and apologised for his behaviour to Witness 2. As mitigating circumstances for Astrit Haraqija, the Trial Chamber considered his good character and his involvement in inclusive and conciliatory political projects as well his family situation. I will now read the relevant part of the disposition of the Judgement. Mr. Haraqija, would you please rise. I do it at the same time, Mr. Morina, would you also please rise. Pursuant to the Statute of the Tribunal and Rules 70 and 77 bis of the Rules, the accused Astrit Haraqija is guilty of contempt of the Tribunal, Count 1, punishable under 77(A)(iv) and Rule 77(G) of the Rules. Astrit Haraqija is hereby sentenced to a single sentence of five months of imprisonment. Astrit Haraqija has been in custody for 36 days and pursuant to Rule 101(C) of the Rules he is entitled to credit for the period of time he has been in custody towards service of the sentence imposed. The accused Bajrush Morina is guilty of contempt of the Tribunal, Count 1, punishable under 77(A)(iv) and Rule 77(G) of the Rules. Bajrush Morina is hereby sentenced to a single sentence of three months of imprisonment. Bajrush Morina has been in custody for 36 days. Pursuant to Rule 101(C) of the Rules, he is entitled to credit for the period of time he has been in custody towards service of the sentence imposed. The registrar is take measures necessary for the enforcement of the sentence. This concludes the deliver of the Judgement, which will now be made publicly available. The Chamber stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it please, Your Honours, two short matters with your leave. Firstly we're grateful for the judgement. There is a right of course articulated in Rule 77(J), a right of appeal. Your Honour, that is, of course, not before Your Honours, but given the Christmas recess, I wonder if in court we could get the agreement of the Prosecution, just for the record, that there will not an objection should we wish to extend that 15 days to start from the new term in the new year. That's the first matter. It's quite discrete, but it may expedite matters when we do file an application under Rule 127 for an extension of time. Your Honour, I'll deal with the second matter, with your leave, after my learned friend Mr. Saxon has responded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution does not agree with the proposition of my learned friend, and believes that the appropriate procedure at this point would be file a motion that can be addressed properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you allow me, Mr. Khan, for the -- the -- this Trial Chamber, of course, I observed what you were asking from Mr. Saxon, that is to have on the record his position in relation to the matter you raised. You will understand that a Trial Chamber is of course not in a position to extend any time-limits for filing appeals. And therefore, it's on the record, but that's all that can be said at this moment. And I will not engage in any discussion at this moment to what extent time-limits, in relation to appeals are of public order and not easily to be changed under Rule -- I think it is it Rule 126 bis or 127 bis. That's being put on the record so that you have no expectations, you could not rely on this Trial Chamber allowing you to raise at the matter at any later stage as to the results of your efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful and, Your Honour, we don't have expectations. I think we're quite reasonable in that regard. The 15 days, of course, does expire on the 2nd of January, but we will make the application in the usual way. Your Honour, the other matter is this sentence of course and this judgement has profound implications for the client. He has previously been granted provisional release by Your Honours. There is, in my submission, a -- a gap in the Rules regarding the precise procedure that should be adopted now. Rule 65, I -- I believe, makes it very clear beyond any doubt that the Appeals Chamber itself can grant provisional release, but it can only grant provision release when it is seized of a matter. It will not be seized of a matter until a notice of appeal is filed. We have 15 days to file that notice of appeal. Your Honour, as a generally principle of law, in my submission, that a decision should be rendered effective. They should not be rendered negatory or devoid of meaning. Given the time my client has served in custody thus far, and given the five-month sentence that has been imposed and the one-month gap, or thereabouts, that is enforced upon the client due to no fault of his own because of the Christmas recess, we ask -- it is my submission that Your Honours do have inherent power under Rule 65 to grant provisional release pending an application to the Appeals Chamber. Your Honour, if we do not have recourse to Your Honours for justice, we do not have recourse at all in a manner that would make an appeal as to the sentence and this -- and I pause there. This is the highest sentence for contempt, as far as I'm aware, that has been -- imposed by this Tribunal in its existence. So, Your Honours, it is my principal submission that Your Honours are empowered, not necessarily under Rule 54 only, but even by the terms of Rule 65, to grant provisional release pending appeal. Your Honour, that is my principal application. Perhaps if my learned friend can respond, I may reply to whatever options he has. But in a nutshell, if we do not have such a right, in effect any appeal would be rendered devoid of meaning and substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: For the Defence of Mr. Bajrush Morina, I would like it join the submissions of my learned friend. Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dieckmann. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution in no way wants to deny a particular procedural right to the Defence. But having said that, we leave it in the Trial Chamber's hands to determine whether the Chamber can take jurisdiction over this matter at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm most grateful for that indication. In that regard then, the submissions that have been addressed and accepted by Your Honours previously are relevant in my submission; namely, that the trial in this case in which the alleged contempt or in which the contempt was committed, according to Your Honours' finding, is ceased. Mr. Haraqija has been previously granted provisional release and there's not been a whisper, there's not been an allegation whatsoever that he has breached any term of the provisional release in the months that he has been free. In those circumstances and given how -- how Draconian in many respects the sentence -- or how great the impact the sentence is on the accused, it is my submission that the margin of discretion must err in the side of his being granted a provisional release pending appeal. Your Honours, unless I can assist you further, those are my principal submissions. Mr. President, if you or Your Honours do have questions, I would be delighted to try to address them; but certainly there has been no difficulty with UNMIK in policing the conditions that have been previously imposed. If the appeal is not successful, and Your Honours have very candidly, even from the summary Judgement read out, acknowledged that this is a novel area of law regarding corroboration. The authorities are not in conformity as to the weight that should be given, and in those circumstances, I would ask that -- Your Honour, in those circumstances I would ask that the application be granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan and Mr. Dieckmann, you have raised the issue of a gap in the rules. The gap between the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber. You have addressed us, and I understand your submissions, and may I take it that Mr. Dieckmann also joins in those submissions, that all circumstances still are as they were before. There is, of course, one difference that there was a judgement now, but I'm confident that you have not ignored that. You have suggested that in this gap that this Trial Chamber would have competence, would have jurisdiction to still decide on requests for release, but let me refrain from saying whether it is provisional or not because there is a judgement, although it still might be appealed, but that we have competence to do so. We'll consider that. If the answer would be in the affirmative, then, of course, we will rule on your request, on your application. However, a gap has always two sides. The Trial Chamber is the one side; the Appeals Chamber is the other side of the gap. And who would fill it in, if either of them would fill in a gap or whether that gap is there for good reasons, is still to be seen. Now, the Trial Chamber advises you that just in case we might feel -- we might determine that we're not competent to deal with the matter, not to ignore and not to neglect the other side of the gap because if we would not be competent to rule on the matter, then most likely at whatever stage it will be the Appeals Chamber. So therefore don't forget the Appeals Chambers in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm most obliged and with your indulgence, two points. It is my respectful submission that at the moment, at this present moment, there is -- well, the gap only arises later on when the Appeals Chamber is seized of the matter. At this moment, the only Court that is seized of this matter is Your Honours. It's this Trial Chamber. You're no longer -- you're still not functus of this case. The written judgement still has not been distributed to the parties, and that was in relation to my principal submission. But Your Honours, your point is well taken that in the event that we're not successful in relation to our primary submission, of course, we are alive to possible remedies to the Appeals Chamber, but the Appeals Chamber has to be seized of the matter. Your Honour, the second point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, if you would please be very brief because it is quite exceptional that we start this kind of matters during a session where a Judgement is delivered, but under the special circumstances, I and the Chamber allowed you to do that. So be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will be extremely brief. Your Honour, there has been cases where suspended sentences have been imposed by a Trial Chamber but this Court. And I think in those circumstances, the Trial Chamber -- and it's not been a matter of controversy, as far as I'm aware, have still been there to police that suspended sentence. Your Honour, the second option, of course, for Your Honours is to grant a stay of execution for the enforcement of a sentence pending any appeal. So there are two procedural devices available --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under which Rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's your inherent powers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Inherent powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I mean, that's your inherent powers. I mean, Your Honours, of course, are intimately familiar with the whole scheme of these Rules, and the way that they were drafted is to deal with the readily anticipated matters that come before Your Honours. Contempt matters, of course, are a subspecies of that, as it were, but I would ask that Your Honours do give the most anxious scrutiny to these two procedural options that I have attempted, however feably, to articulate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider the matter. Finally, I would like to apologise to you, Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: No worries. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber stands adjourned.
